facts.label: Source-by-source assessment
facts.text: 1. 10-K for FY2025 (10-K_2025-12-31_crwv-20251231.htm.jsonl): audited annual statements for CoreWeave, Inc. on a consolidated basis in USD millions. Debt note at pages:175-182 lists facilities with maturities and effective rates. It is the base for the FY2025 comparatives. The cover states the registrant is a non-accelerated filer and the text discloses material weaknesses in internal control (page:83). 2. 10-Q for Q3 2025 (10-Q_2025-09-30_crwv-20250930.htm.jsonl): provides the discrete Q3 2025 quarter and the nine months 2025 base. It is expressed in thousands, whereas the later files are in millions. It is a separate active source and is not a duplicate of any other file. 3. 10-Q for Q1 2026 (10-Q_2026-03-31_crwv-20260331.htm.jsonl): provides the discrete Q1 2026 quarter, its own debt table (page:24), liquidity table (page:46) and a subsequent event on the April 2026 convertible notes (page:40). It is separate from the Q2 file; Q2 does not replace it, because Q2 gives six-month cash flows only. 4. 10-Q for Q2 2026 (10-Q_2026-06-30_crwv-20260630.htm.jsonl): the latest filed statements and the controlling source for the June 30, 2026 balance sheet, debt, liquidity and leases. It states the August 2026 events. 5. Q4 2025 release: attributed management claims and non-GAAP reconciliations, plus the discrete Q4 2025 quarter that the filings do not isolate. 6. Q1 2026 release: same family; supports discrete Q1 2026 non-GAAP measures. 7. Q2 2026 release: same family; supports discrete Q2 2026 non-GAAP measures and the discrete Q2 2026 cash flow. A management claim in a release cannot override a filing; where the two differ the filing controls.

facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: The financial base is sufficient to describe the June 30, 2026 position and the path from FY2025, with stated limits. The audited FY2025 statements, three quarterly filings and three releases tie to each other: six months 2026 revenue of $4,653 million equals Q1 2026 plus Q2 2026, and the debt table sums to the printed total. The picture is of fast, debt-financed growth. Revenue in Q2 2026 was $2,575 million against $1,212 million a year earlier, adjusted EBITDA was $1,510 million, but the company still reported an operating loss of $(49) million and net interest expense of $(640) million in the quarter. Principal debt of $35,551 million (about 89.5 percent recourse by principal, calculated below) is mostly secured, project-level delayed-draw debt plus unsecured notes and convertibles. Leverage on LTM adjusted EBITDA is 8.08x gross and 6.82x net of unrestricted cash and marketable securities, and cash interest cover is 3.35x; both are flattered by the EBITDA definition (it adds back stock compensation and acquisition costs, and is struck after operating lease cost, so lease cost is not in the add-backs) and by cash interest being net of capitalized interest. Debt at period end also funds assets not yet earning revenue, so period-end debt over trailing earnings overstates run-rate leverage, and the contracted backlog (remaining performance obligations of $103.7 billion) is the offsetting evidence. The main restrictions are that financial covenant levels are not printed, so headroom is Not calculable, that guarantors are not named, and that nothing after the Q2 2026 filing except the August 2026 events in the filing note is in the pack.

facts.label: Revenue durability
facts.text: Evidence: committed contracts were 98% of Q2 2026 revenue with a weighted-average duration of about five years and 103.7 billion of remaining performance obligations. Mechanic: take-or-pay terms fix revenue for the term, so debt service is supported by contracted cash flows, but the backlog converts only as data center power and equipment are delivered and available; 393 MW remain undelivered at one leased site. Implication: refinancing risk is lowest where facilities are backed by delivered, contracted capacity, and highest for undelivered capacity financed ahead of contracts.
facts.basis: Literal handoff table; no financial reinterpretation.

Implication: operating loss in Q2 2026 and negative free cash flow in the financial base handoff leave debt service dependent on prepayments and new financing.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: CoreWeave sells GPU-based AI cloud capacity, mostly through multi-year take-or-pay contracts, and finances the equipment and data center build-out with asset-level debt backed by those contracts, supplemented by corporate notes, convertibles and equity. The evidence supports a creditor view built on three mechanics. First, revenue visibility is long: committed contracts have a weighted-average duration of about five years, and the filing reports a large contracted backlog, but that backlog converts to revenue only as capacity is delivered and made available, and the filings disclose power still undelivered at leased sites. Second, concentration is the main operating risk: a handful of customers account for most revenue, named customers include Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and Jane Street, and the identity of the top customers changes between filings. Third, funding is the main structural risk: each growth step is paid for by new debt or equity, and the debt mixes recourse parent obligations, parent-guaranteed subsidiary facilities and one non-recourse facility, so the claim a creditor holds depends on which entity borrowed and who guaranteed. Ownership is public with founders holding control through a ten-vote share class; no sponsor is named, and no ownership percentages are disclosed in the sources read. Documented issuer behaviour is mostly supportive (equity issued alongside debt) and otherwise neutral; no dividend recapitalization, priming or uptier is documented in the pages read, but the executed documents that would show what is permitted are not supplied. Management claims in releases (power, backlog, partnerships) are attributed and not adopted.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: There is no merger, buyout or sponsor transaction in the sources. The transaction content is a financing programme, set out in date order with status as of the filing of the Q2 2026 quarterly report, and the figures match the financial base handoff. In January 2026 NVIDIA bought about 23 million Class A shares for 2.0 billion gross (completed). In March 2026 a subsidiary, CoreWeave Compute Acquisition Co. VIII, LLC, signed the DDTL 4.0 facility of 8.5 billion with MUFG Bank as administrative agent, available for draws to June 30, 2027 and maturing in March 2032 (10-Q 2026-06-30, pages:28-29); it is non-recourse apart from limited carve-out guarantees, is secured on the equity and substantially all assets of that subsidiary, and had 2,837 million outstanding at June 30, 2026 (CP-1). Floating loans bear SOFR plus 2.25% and fixed loans bear 2.00% over a Treasury-based rate. In April 2026 the company issued 2.8 billion of 9.75% senior notes due October 2031 (2,750 million principal) and 4.0 billion of 1.75% convertible senior notes due October 2032 (conversion price about 119.60, no redemption before October 8, 2029, capped calls costing 492 million with a cap price of 230.00); a portion of the convertible proceeds funded the capped calls, the remainder is for general corporate purposes, and the senior note proceeds were retained for general corporate purposes (10-Q 2026-06-30, pages:32-33). The revolver was repaid in April 2026 and convertible promissory notes of 172 million principal (168 million carrying at December 31, 2025) were settled in shares at 106.61 per share (pages:31 and 34). In May 2026 CoreWeave Financing DDTL V, LLC signed the DDTL 5.0 facility of 3.1 billion with Morgan Stanley as administrative agent at SOFR plus 4.50%, drawable to September 30, 2026, repayable monthly from November 2026, guaranteed by the parent and secured on subsidiary equity and assets, with 1,101 million outstanding at June 30, 2026 (page:30). In June 2026 the company issued 1.3 billion of 9.625% senior notes due July 2032 and 2.0 billion euro of 8.50% senior notes due July 2032, hedged with a cross currency swap, with proceeds retained for general corporate purposes (pages:19 and 33-34). Notes are unsecured and guaranteed by certain wholly-owned subsidiaries (page:134). The financing is part of a layered structure: recourse parent debt, parent-guaranteed single-purpose facilities, and non-recourse debt; liquidity effect was cash of 5,524 million at June 30, 2026 against 2,244 million at March 31, 2026 (CP-1). After the quarter, in August 2026, the company signed the DDTL 5.5 facility of 2.6 billion with JPMorgan as agent at SOFR plus 5.5%, maturing September 2031, drawable to December 2026, and drew 1.2 billion; it also drew 1.2 billion on the revolver (page:46). Uses: delayed draw facilities finance computing equipment purchases, subject to debt-sizing limits tied to the cost of eligible assets; notes and convertibles fund general corporate purposes. Status of each: completed and drawn, except undrawn commitments (DDTL 4.0, DDTL 5.0 and DDTL 5.5 balances), which depend on eligible asset purchases. Off-balance-sheet lease and joint venture commitments (35.5 billion of leases not yet commenced, 1.7 billion of joint venture funding) sit alongside the debt and are in the financial base handoff. Conflicts and limits: the DDTL 5.0 maturity is printed as November 2031 in the debt table and as an expected final payment in May 2031 in the text, logged below and not reconciled; the sources do not contain the indentures or credit agreements, so use-of-proceeds restrictions, guarantor lists and covenants are Not supplied.

facts.label: Calculations
facts.text: 1. Voting weight. Class B votes = shares x 10 and Class A votes = shares x 1; Class C has none. July 31, 2026: 92,664,912 x 10 = 926,649,120; plus 458,871,690 Class A = 1,385,520,810 total votes; Class B share = 926,649,120 / 1,385,520,810 = 66.9%. January 31, 2026: 106,660,052 x 10 = 1,066,600,520; plus 419,028,081 = 1,485,628,601; Class B share = 71.8%. Assumes the cover-page counts are the votes outstanding and ignores unvested awards. Not a company-disclosed percentage; the co-founders also hold some Class A shares, which are not disclosed in the sources read. 2. Customer concentration: 36 + 26 + 10 = 72 percent of Q2 2026 revenue (same as CP-1). United States share of Q2 2026 revenue = 2,389 / 2,575 = 92.8 percent. 3. Monolith notes: 185 million issued less 13 million with vesting conditions = 172 million, equal to the 172 million of convertible promissory notes in the Q2 2026 10-Q; the link between the two is an analyst reading, as the 10-Q does not name the acquiree. 4. No other calculation. All debt, liquidity and lease figures are those of the financial base handoff.

facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: CoreWeave, Inc. is a high-risk credit: its contracted demand is strong, but its balance sheet depends on continued access to new debt and equity. The strongest support is revenue visibility, with committed contracts at 98% of Q2 2026 revenue and remaining performance obligations of USD 103.7 billion. The weakest point is financial: principal debt of USD 35,551 million at June 30, 2026 is 8.08x LTM adjusted EBITDA, and six months 2026 free cash flow was USD (10,454) million. The outcome will be decided by delivery and funding: whether CoreWeave brings contracted capacity online on time, collects from a concentrated customer base, and refinances USD 4,413 million due in the remainder of 2026 and USD 6,184 million in 2027 while delayed-draw commitments stay conditional.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: First, leverage is high and rising faster than earnings. CoreWeave had principal debt of USD 35,551 million at June 30, 2026 against USD 21,615 million at December 31, 2025, and LTM adjusted EBITDA of USD 4,400 million, giving 8.08x gross and 6.82x net of unrestricted cash and marketable securities, against 6.99x and 5.97x at year end [Documentary Fact; financial base]. Cash interest cover on adjusted EBITDA is 3.35x, or 2.35x against net interest expense of USD 1,874 million. Both ratios flatter the position: adjusted EBITDA adds back stock compensation, cash interest is net of capitalized interest of USD 322 million over the twelve months, and on operating income plus depreciation and amortization gross leverage is 9.46x [Analyst Interpretation]. Mechanism: debt funds assets that are not yet earning, so period-end debt over trailing earnings overstates run-rate leverage, but operating income is already negative after interest-bearing growth, with an LTM operating loss of USD (231) million and the LTM net loss is USD (1,928) million.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Second, cash flow does not cover investment. Six months 2026 operating cash flow was USD 3,663 million against purchases of property and equipment of USD 14,117 million, leaving free cash flow of USD (10,454) million; the twelve-month figure is USD (13,655) million [Documentary Fact]. The gap is funded by new debt, equity placements of USD 2.0 billion (NVIDIA, January 2026) and USD 1.0 billion (April 2026), and customer prepayments, with deferred revenue at USD 9,692 million [Documentary Fact]. Implication: the credit relies on markets staying open; a funding pause would force a cut in capital spending and slow the delivery that converts backlog to revenue.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Third, liquidity is large on paper and conditional in practice. Company-reported total liquidity was USD 15,553 million at June 30, 2026: cash USD 5,524 million, marketable securities USD 15 million and availability USD 10,014 million, which rebuilds as USD 1,967 million on the revolver, USD 385 million on DDTL 3.0, USD 5,663 million on DDTL 4.0 and USD 1,999 million on DDTL 5.0 [Documentary Fact]. Draws on the delayed-draw facilities are limited to eligible asset purchases, the DDTL 3.0 and DDTL 5.0 draw periods ended before the as-of date, and restricted cash of USD 1,380 million sits outside the figure. In August 2026, after the quarter, CoreWeave drew USD 1.2 billion on the revolver and USD 1.2 billion on the new DDTL 5.5 facility, which lowers revolver availability (USD 767 million on the financial base's indicative basis) and means cash and availability at the as-of date are Not calculable [Analyst Interpretation].

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Fourth, the maturity profile is front-loaded relative to cash. Scheduled principal is USD 4,413 million in the remainder of 2026, USD 6,184 million in 2027, USD 4,416 million in 2028, USD 2,421 million in 2029, USD 3,221 million in 2030 and USD 14,896 million after that; current debt is USD 7,513 million against cash of USD 5,524 million [Documentary Fact]. Much of the near-term amount is scheduled amortization on asset-level facilities and equipment financing, which is likely to be serviced from contracted cash flows rather than refinanced [Analyst Interpretation], but DDTL 4.0 payment timing is a management estimate. Implication: near-term refinancing risk is real but concentrated in amortizing secured debt; the unsecured and convertible notes mature from 2030 onward.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Fifth, revenue visibility is strong but concentrated and delivery-dependent. Committed contracts have a weighted-average duration of about five years, remaining performance obligations are USD 103.7 billion with 41% due within 24 months, and management cites a wider backlog of about USD 104 billion plus more than USD 25 billion of commitments added in early Q3 [Documentary Fact and Management Language, kept apart]. Three customers supplied 36%, 26% and 10% of Q2 2026 revenue (72% together), customers A and B were 32% each of receivables, and customer labels change between periods, so the fall from 71% for one customer a year earlier is not a like-for-like trend [Documentary Fact]. Mechanism: take-or-pay terms fix revenue, but revenue is recognized only as capacity is delivered (393 MW undelivered at one leased site), and service credits reduce the backlog. Implication: counterparty quality of a few customers drives default risk for the asset-level facilities.

facts.text: Sixth, claims outside the debt figure are large. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Seventh, structure and control limit what a creditor can verify. About 89.5% of principal debt is recourse (USD 31,832 million) and USD 3,719 million is non-recourse; delayed-draw facilities are secured on subsidiary assets and guaranteed by the parent except DDTL 4.0, while the notes are unsecured and guaranteed by unnamed subsidiaries [Documentary Fact]. Founders hold all Class B shares, which carry about 66.9% of votes on the cover-page counts, and no sponsor is named [Analyst Interpretation]. Mechanism: asset-level lenders hold first-priority liens on the financed equipment and cash flows, so value available to unsecured holders depends on residual value after those claims; this is a mechanic, not a recovery conclusion. Material weaknesses in internal control continued at June 30, 2026 and securities suits are pending with no accrual.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. CoreWeave has long contracted revenue: committed contracts are 98% of Q2 2026 revenue and remaining performance obligations are USD 103.7 billion with a weighted-average contract duration of about five years [Documentary Fact]. It has grown fast, with Q2 2026 revenue of USD 2,575 million against USD 1,212 million a year earlier, up 112.5%, and LTM revenue of USD 7,590 million [Documentary Fact]. It has shown access to several funding sources in 2026, including secured delayed-draw loans, unsecured notes, convertibles, a euro bond and two equity placements, which supports refinancing capacity while markets stay open [Analyst Interpretation]. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 58.0% over the last twelve months [Documentary Fact; management measure]. The asset-level structure ties each facility to financed assets and contracted cash flows, with the parent guaranteeing all but DDTL 4.0 [Documentary Fact]. Counterparties named in the sources include Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and Jane Street, with commitments of up to about USD 6.5 billion, USD 21.0 billion and USD 6.0 billion for the last three [Documentary Fact].

Refinancing and amortization are near term, with USD 4,413 million and USD 6,184 million due in the remainder of 2026 and 2027 [Documentary Fact]. Material weaknesses in internal control continue, which weakens the reliability of figures used in lender tests [Documentary Fact]. Stockholders' equity of USD 5,024 million is small against principal debt of USD 35,551 million [Documentary Fact]. Covenant levels, guarantors and financing documents are not supplied, so headroom and legal protections cannot be tested [Insufficient Information].

rows.label: CoreWeave is a high-risk credit: contracted revenue is long and large, but principal debt of USD 35,551 million is 8.08x LTM adjusted EBITDA, free cash flow is deeply negative and funding depends on continued market access.
Remaining performance obligations of USD 103.7 billion and committed contracts at 98% of Q2 2026 revenue give long revenue visibility.
Principal debt rose from USD 21,615 million to USD 35,551 million in six months, while LTM adjusted EBITDA is USD 4,400 million.
Six months 2026 free cash flow was USD (10,454) million, funded by new debt, equity placements and customer prepayments.
Reported availability of USD 10,014 million is conditional, and USD 4,413 million of debt matures in the remainder of 2026.
Three customers supplied 72% of Q2 2026 revenue and founder-held Class B shares carry about 66.9% of votes.

spans.text: ## Request

Module: source readiness for CoreWeave, Inc. (ticker CRWV, Delaware registrant, SEC file number 001-42563). As-of date: 2026-11-05. Evidence cutoff: 2026-11-05. Pathway: credit snapshot, public case. Reporting currency per the run context: USD. Current period per the run context: Q2 2026 (quarter ended 2026-06-30). Prior period per the run context: FY2025.

Question answered: can the seven pinned issuer sources support the requested downstream work (the fundamental data module, the business and transaction module, the credit synthesis and the evidence trace review), and what remains blocked? This module gives no credit conclusion, no legal interpretation and no investment opinion. It does not normalize, reconcile or calculate figures. Source sufficiency is separate from completion of downstream analysis.

Perimeter: the registrant is CoreWeave, Inc., the ultimate parent. The context names no borrower, parent, guarantor or sponsor (all blank), so none is assumed. The Q2 2026 quarterly filing states that debt is split into recourse and non-recourse, and that guarantors of the notes are certain wholly-owned subsidiaries that are not named in the pinned text (see Gaps).

### Financial base view

The financial base is sufficient to describe the June 30, 2026 position and the path from FY2025, with stated limits. The audited FY2025 statements, three quarterly filings and three releases tie to each other: six months 2026 revenue of $4,653 million equals Q1 2026 plus Q2 2026, and the debt table sums to the printed total. The picture is of fast, debt-financed growth. Revenue in Q2 2026 was $2,575 million against $1,212 million a year earlier, adjusted EBITDA was $1,510 million, but the company still reported an operating loss of $(49) million and net interest expense of $(640) million in the quarter. Principal debt of $35,551 million (about 89.5 percent recourse by principal, calculated below) is mostly secured, project-level delayed-draw debt plus unsecured notes and convertibles. Leverage on LTM adjusted EBITDA is 8.08x gross and 6.82x net of unrestricted cash and marketable securities, and cash interest cover is 3.35x; both are flattered by the EBITDA definition (it adds back stock compensation and acquisition costs, and is struck after operating lease cost, so lease cost is not in the add-backs) and by cash interest being net of capitalized interest. Debt at period end also funds assets not yet earning revenue, so period-end debt over trailing earnings overstates run-rate leverage, and the contracted backlog (remaining performance obligations of $103.7 billion) is the offsetting evidence. The main restrictions are that financial covenant levels are not printed, so headroom is Not calculable, that guarantors are not named, and that nothing after the Q2 2026 filing except the August 2026 events in the filing note is in the pack.

### Liquidity and covenants

Liquidity at June 30, 2026, from printed inputs: unrestricted cash and cash equivalents 5,524 plus marketable securities 15 plus reported availability 10,014 equals the company's total liquidity of 15,553. The availability of 10,014 reconciles exactly to the facilities the risk factor names: revolver 2,500 capacity less 533 letters of credit gives 1,967; DDTL 3.0 up to 2,600 less 2,215 outstanding gives 385; DDTL 4.0 of 8,500 less 2,837 outstanding gives 5,663; DDTL 5.0 of 3,100 less 1,101 outstanding gives 1,999. Cash is partly restricted: restricted cash of 1,380 sits outside the figure. Commitment periods ending within twelve months of June 30, 2026: DDTL 3.0 draw period (July 2026, per the 10-K), DDTL 5.0 draw period (September 30, 2026) and DDTL 4.0 commitments (June 30, 2027); DDTL 5.0 amortization also starts in November 2026. The revolver matures November 2029. Because DDTL draws are limited to a percentage of the depreciable cost of eligible equipment and project-level conditions, availability is not freely drawable cash.

Covenants: no financial maintenance test, level, step-down or reported ratio is printed in any pinned source, so headroom is Not calculable. What is printed: the company was in compliance with all covenants under its delayed draw term loan agreements at June 30, 2026 (10-Q page:31); the revolver was amended in November 2025 "to modify certain covenant metrics" (10-K page:180); risk factors state the company is "required to maintain specified financial covenant ratios" (10-Q page:137, 10-K page:96); DDTL 4.0 requires restricted cash based on a forward-looking three-month coverage of scheduled cash interest and principal payments, periodic swap settlements and operating expenses (10-Q page:30); DDTL 4.0 and 5.0 require interest rate hedges on at least 95 percent of reasonably anticipated floating-rate borrowings (pages:29-30); debt sizing for DDTL 4.0 references projected debt service coverage (page:29). Differences from the metrics computed here: any lender definition of EBITDA, leverage or coverage is not supplied, and the ratios above use the company's non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA.

## Calculations

1. LTM June 2026 for any flow = FY2025 plus six months 2026 less six months 2025.

- Interest expense, net: 1,229 + 1,176 - 531 = 1,874.
- Capitalized interest: 182 + 176 - 36 = 322.
- Cash paid for interest: 869 + 806 - 362 = 1,313.
- Purchase of property and equipment: 10,309 + 14,117 - 3,860 = 20,566.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| CoreWeave is a fast-growing AI cloud operator with long take-or-pay contracts, heavy customer concentration, founder voting control and layered asset-level and unsecured debt. | Medium | Executed financing documents, guarantor lists, ownership percentages and guidance are not in the sources, so control rights and recovery mechanics cannot be assessed. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Revenue is mostly take-or-pay: committed contracts were 98% of Q2 2026 revenue and unsatisfied remaining performance obligations were $103.7 billion. | Revenue visibility is long, but conversion depends on delivering data center power and equipment on time. | Medium |

| Three customers supplied 36%, 26% and 10% of Q2 2026 revenue, against 71% from one customer in Q2 2025. | Concentration is lower but still high; one customer's delay or non-payment would hit debt service quickly. | High |

| Growth is funded by customer prepayments, asset-level secured debt, unsecured notes, convertibles and equity placements, including $2.0 billion from NVIDIA in January 2026. | Funding is diversified but needs continued market access; financed assets secure asset-level debt while the notes are unsecured. | Medium |

| Founders hold all Class B shares, which carry ten votes each; no sponsor is named and no ownership percentages are disclosed in the sources. | Control sits with founders and public-equity investors, not a sponsor, so creditor protection rests on documents not supplied. | Medium |

| Material weaknesses in internal control continued at June 30, 2026, and securities class action and derivative suits were filed in 2026. | Reporting reliability and litigation need monitoring; no loss is accrued and none can be estimated. | Medium |
### Business and transaction view

CoreWeave sells GPU-based AI cloud capacity, mostly through multi-year take-or-pay contracts, and finances the equipment and data center build-out with asset-level debt backed by those contracts, supplemented by corporate notes, convertibles and equity. The evidence supports a creditor view built on three mechanics. First, revenue visibility is long: committed contracts have a weighted-average duration of about five years, and the filing reports a large contracted backlog, but that backlog converts to revenue only as capacity is delivered and made available, and the filings disclose power still undelivered at leased sites. Second, concentration is the main operating risk: a handful of customers account for most revenue, named customers include Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and Jane Street, and the identity of the top customers changes between filings. Third, funding is the main structural risk: each growth step is paid for by new debt or equity, and the debt mixes recourse parent obligations, parent-guaranteed subsidiary facilities and one non-recourse facility, so the claim a creditor holds depends on which entity borrowed and who guaranteed. Ownership is public with founders holding control through a ten-vote share class; no sponsor is named, and no ownership percentages are disclosed in the sources read. Documented issuer behaviour is mostly supportive (equity issued alongside debt) and otherwise neutral; no dividend recapitalization, priming or uptier is documented in the pages read, but the executed documents that would show what is permitted are not supplied. Management claims in releases (power, backlog, partnerships) are attributed and not adopted.

There is no merger, buyout or sponsor transaction in the sources. The transaction content is a financing programme, set out in date order with status as of the filing of the Q2 2026 quarterly report, and the figures match the financial base handoff. In January 2026 NVIDIA bought about 23 million Class A shares for 2.0 billion gross (completed). In March 2026 a subsidiary, CoreWeave Compute Acquisition Co. VIII, LLC, signed the DDTL 4.0 facility of 8.5 billion with MUFG Bank as administrative agent, available for draws to June 30, 2027 and maturing in March 2032 (10-Q 2026-06-30, pages:28-29); it is non-recourse apart from limited carve-out guarantees, is secured on the equity and substantially all assets of that subsidiary, and had 2,837 million outstanding at June 30, 2026 (CP-1). Floating loans bear SOFR plus 2.25% and fixed loans bear 2.00% over a Treasury-based rate. In April 2026 the company issued 2.8 billion of 9.75% senior notes due October 2031 (2,750 million principal) and 4.0 billion of 1.75% convertible senior notes due October 2032 (conversion price about 119.60, no redemption before October 8, 2029, capped calls costing 492 million with a cap price of 230.00); a portion of the convertible proceeds funded the capped calls, the remainder is for general corporate purposes, and the senior note proceeds were retained for general corporate purposes (10-Q 2026-06-30, pages:32-33). The revolver was repaid in April 2026 and convertible promissory notes of 172 million principal (168 million carrying at December 31, 2025) were settled in shares at 106.61 per share (pages:31 and 34). In May 2026 CoreWeave Financing DDTL V, LLC signed the DDTL 5.0 facility of 3.1 billion with Morgan Stanley as administrative agent at SOFR plus 4.50%, drawable to September 30, 2026, repayable monthly from November 2026, guaranteed by the parent and secured on subsidiary equity and assets, with 1,101 million outstanding at June 30, 2026 (page:30). In June 2026 the company issued 1.3 billion of 9.625% senior notes due July 2032 and 2.0 billion euro of 8.50% senior notes due July 2032, hedged with a cross currency swap, with proceeds retained for general corporate purposes (pages:19 and 33-34). Notes are unsecured and guaranteed by certain wholly-owned subsidiaries (page:134). The financing is part of a layered structure: recourse parent debt, parent-guaranteed single-purpose facilities, and non-recourse debt; liquidity effect was cash of 5,524 million at June 30, 2026 against 2,244 million at March 31, 2026 (CP-1). After the quarter, in August 2026, the company signed the DDTL 5.5 facility of 2.6 billion with JPMorgan as agent at SOFR plus 5.5%, maturing September 2031, drawable to December 2026, and drew 1.2 billion; it also drew 1.2 billion on the revolver (page:46). Uses: delayed draw facilities finance computing equipment purchases, subject to debt-sizing limits tied to the cost of eligible assets; notes and convertibles fund general corporate purposes. Status of each: completed and drawn, except undrawn commitments (DDTL 4.0, DDTL 5.0 and DDTL 5.5 balances), which depend on eligible asset purchases. Off-balance-sheet lease and joint venture commitments (35.5 billion of leases not yet commenced, 1.7 billion of joint venture funding) sit alongside the debt and are in the financial base handoff. Conflicts and limits: the DDTL 5.0 maturity is printed as November 2031 in the debt table and as an expected final payment in May 2031 in the text, logged below and not reconciled; the sources do not contain the indentures or credit agreements, so use-of-proceeds restrictions, guarantor lists and covenants are Not supplied.
### Logged conflicts
| Topic | Span one | Span two | Effect | Resolution |

| Backlog measure | Q2 2026 release, page:1: "Revenue backlog1 was approximately $104 billion as of June 30, 2026." | 10-Q 2026-06-30, page:15: "the Company had $103.7 billion of unsatisfied RPO" | Different definitions of contracted revenue; the filing controls for remaining performance obligations | Logged, not reconciled |

| DDTL 5.0 final maturity | 10-Q 2026-06-30, page:26: "DDTL 5.0 Facility Nov 2031 9% 1,101" | 10-Q 2026-06-30, page:30: "with the expected final payment due in May 2031" | Maturity wall timing for about 1.1 billion of principal differs by six months | Logged, not reconciled |

| DDTL 2.1 maturity | 10-K, page:175: "DDTL 2.1 Facility December 2030 9 % 2,741" | 10-Q 2026-06-30, page:26: "DDTL 2.1 Facility Mar 2031 9% 3,000" | Date moved between filings; reason not stated | Logged, not reconciled |

| Customer labels | 10-Q 2026-06-30, page:14: "The customer references of A through D may represent different customers than those reported in a previous period." | 10-Q 2026-06-30, page:72: "approximately 71% of our revenue from our top customer for the three months ended June 30, 2025" | The 71% prior-year customer may not be the 36% current-year Customer A, so a trend in one customer's share is not established | Logged, not reconciled |
### Credit translations
| Theme | Evidence, risk mechanic and credit implication | Counter-evidence or conflict |

| Revenue durability | Evidence: committed contracts were 98% of Q2 2026 revenue with a weighted-average duration of about five years and 103.7 billion of remaining performance obligations. Mechanic: take-or-pay terms fix revenue for the term, so debt service is supported by contracted cash flows, but the backlog converts only as data center power and equipment are delivered and available; 393 MW remain undelivered at one leased site. Implication: refinancing risk is lowest where facilities are backed by delivered, contracted capacity, and highest for undelivered capacity financed ahead of contracts. | Backlog is net of variable consideration such as service credits; logged conflict on the backlog measure. |

| Margin and cash-flow risk | Evidence: cost of revenue rose to 34% of revenue from 26%, and technology and infrastructure expense is dominated by depreciation. Mechanic: rent, power and depreciation scale with deployed capacity, so margins compress while new sites are not yet earning. Implication: operating loss in Q2 2026 and negative free cash flow in the financial base handoff leave debt service dependent on prepayments and new financing. | Prepayments typically at contract inception partly fund the build. |

| Concentration risk | Evidence: the top three customers were 36%, 26% and 10% of Q2 2026 revenue; customers A and B were each 32% of receivables. Mechanic: a few counterparties carry most receivables and contracted revenue, so a delay or dispute stalls cash conversion for the asset-level facilities. Implication: single-name credit quality of hyperscale and AI-lab customers is a first-order driver of loss given default. | Customer labels change between periods (logged conflict); named counterparties are large. |

| Sponsor and control | Evidence: founders hold all Class B shares with ten votes each; no sponsor; public investors including NVIDIA supplied equity. Mechanic: no sponsor equity cure or support agreement is documented; control sits with founders, and equity support depends on market access. Implication: creditor protection depends on documents not supplied. | Equity placements in January and April 2026 are documented support. |

| Structure and guarantees | Evidence: parent notes are unsecured and guaranteed by certain subsidiaries; delayed-draw facilities are secured on subsidiary assets and guaranteed by the parent except DDTL 4.0. Mechanic: asset-level lenders hold first-priority liens on the financed equipment and cash flows, the notes do not, and guarantor identities are unknown. Implication: recovery for noteholders depends on residual value after asset-level claims; no recovery conclusion is drawn. | Guarantor list and indentures are not supplied. |

| Key uncertainties | Evidence: continuing material weaknesses, securities class action and derivative suits with no estimable loss, supplier dependence on NVIDIA GPUs, and 35.5 billion of leases not yet commenced. Mechanic: control weaknesses reduce reliability of reported figures that covenants and sizing tests use. Implication: monitoring posture should include the compliance certificates and sizing tests that the sources do not contain. | No loss accrued. |
### Consumers
| Module | Readiness | What it should take from this module | Why it matters | Gap and required action |
| CP-1 | Complete before this module | Nothing new; this module consumed its debt, liquidity and commitment figures | The business facts explain the financial base | None |

| CP-2 | Ready with limitations | Revenue durability, concentration, structure, control and uncertainty rows; the logged conflicts | The synthesis must connect contracted revenue to debt service and name the limits on recovery mechanics | Guarantors, covenants and ownership percentages Not supplied; action: state them as gaps, do not infer |

| CP-5 | Ready with limitations | Each quoted row with its locator; the four logged conflicts | The evidence trace must resolve each quote to its page | Management claims in releases are attributed; check that they stay tagged as Management Language |
## Calculations

1. Voting weight. Class B votes = shares x 10 and Class A votes = shares x 1; Class C has none. July 31, 2026: 92,664,912 x 10 = 926,649,120; plus 458,871,690 Class A = 1,385,520,810 total votes; Class B share = 926,649,120 / 1,385,520,810 = 66.9%. January 31, 2026: 106,660,052 x 10 = 1,066,600,520; plus 419,028,081 = 1,485,628,601; Class B share = 71.8%. Assumes the cover-page counts are the votes outstanding and ignores unvested awards. Not a company-disclosed percentage; the co-founders also hold some Class A shares, which are not disclosed in the sources read.
2. Customer concentration: 36 + 26 + 10 = 72 percent of Q2 2026 revenue (same as CP-1). United States share of Q2 2026 revenue = 2,389 / 2,575 = 92.8 percent.

3. Monolith notes: 185 million issued less 13 million with vesting conditions = 172 million, equal to the 172 million of convertible promissory notes in the Q2 2026 10-Q; the link between the two is an analyst reading, as the 10-Q does not name the acquiree.
4. No other calculation. All debt, liquidity and lease figures are those of the financial base handoff.
## Gaps

1. Executed financing documents (indentures, credit agreements, parent guarantee, intercreditor terms): Not supplied; they are listed as exhibits. Severity high. Affects covenants, guarantor scope, liens, restricted payments and anything on recovery. Remediation: obtain the exhibits.
2. Guarantor list and condensed guarantor financial information: Not supplied. Severity high.
3. Beneficial ownership percentages and holders above 5%: Not supplied (proxy statement not in the pack). Severity medium.
4. Ratings: Not supplied. Severity medium.

5. Customer contract terms (termination rights, pricing, take-or-pay remedies, prepayment amounts by customer) and customer identity for the current top three: Not supplied. Severity high for revenue durability.
6. Management guidance and call transcript: Not supplied. Severity medium.
7. Third quarter 2026 results and events from the filing of the Q2 2026 report to the cutoff: Not supplied. Severity high; the as-of date is 2026-11-05.

8. Monitoring inputs absent: covenant compliance certificates, borrowing-base or sizing calculations for the delayed-draw facilities, add-back bridge for lenders, and a debt-by-entity schedule. Severity high.
9. The relationship between the 1 billion April 2026 share placement and the Jane Street strategic investment is not stated. Severity low.
10. Q3 2025 10-Q and the Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 releases were reviewed for events and attributed claims only.
11. External material: none outside the pinned sources was used. The sector label is from the run context.
## Next module
Proceed to the credit synthesis (CP-2) using both handoffs. Carry forward:

1. Drivers: revenue durability from take-or-pay terms and remaining performance obligations; concentration; funding dependence; structure (parent notes unsecured, asset-level facilities secured and mostly parent-guaranteed, one non-recourse facility); founder control; continuing material weaknesses and litigation.
2. Limits to restate: no covenants, no guarantor list, no ownership percentages, no ratings, no guidance, no third quarter 2026 data, no customer contract terms.
3. Conflicts to name, not reconcile: backlog versus remaining performance obligations; DDTL 5.0 and DDTL 2.1 maturity dates; customer labels across periods.
4. Prohibited: no peer ranking, no instrument recommendation and no expected recovery outcome.
Then run the evidence trace review across all modules.

spans.text: ## Request

This module gives the fundamental credit view of CoreWeave, Inc. (CRWV) as of 2026-11-05, on the credit snapshot pathway, from the creditor perspective. It synthesises the financial base and the business and transaction context only, in USD, with Q2 2026 as the current period and FY2025 as the prior period. It states no peer ranking, no instrument recommendation and no expected recovery outcome.
## Sources
### Issuer sources
This module read no source text. The seven pinned issuer sources below were relied on only through the three handoffs, which quote them with locators.
| Source name | sha256 |
| EX-99.1_2026-02-26_coreweave4q25earningspress.htm.jsonl | d1cb2e7f415a836bfc361c60f3592d7d5ff529dbcae4e476b1fc937be4fb40b5 |
| EX-99.1_2026-05-07_coreweave1q26earningspress.htm.jsonl | e0f8ee20aa75c8abb15cd88aa7bc89813b32cc2ad3558378d8026da7d76cfee8 |
| EX-99.1_2026-08-11_coreweave2q26earningspress.htm.jsonl | af17b6e32fc6d5e125e64130df944ece5d560c39bdc4236cbad0414accede85b |
Context file (settings, not issuer evidence): sha256 98f66cde15d4d68ac95da915aeb204ed4c29c1430841991cd3be8e950d45a9a2.
### Handoffs
| Module | sha256 | How it was consumed |
| CP-0 | 0a718ae2802587f76f44cc2a61e8815a4a88834928edca0479e39f7d34976401 | Opened and read. Source readiness was ready with limitations; its gap list is carried into the gaps below. |

| CP-1 | df2a422a4928d9e15d084ff62a177ff909f3a1e751a2512de167ccad6229229c | Opened and read in full. The financial base: statements, debt, liquidity, maturities, leases and commitments, and the leverage, cover and liquidity measures. Every financial figure below is taken from it. |

| CP-1A | 15e6d01a799b4eadec41d419b7f13d7008399c50166b31b64beabfb6f8b5e942 | Opened and read in full. The business, ownership, governance, transaction and conflict registers. Every business fact below is taken from it. |

Consistency check against the handoffs: the figures in CP-1 and CP-1A agree where they overlap (customer shares, remaining performance obligations of USD 103.7 billion, the financing programme and the DDTL balances). Corrections: none needed. CP-0 treated cash income taxes as unavailable and CP-1 corrected that for FY2025; this module does not use cash taxes.

Category tags used below: Documentary Fact (a CP-1 figure or a CP-1A Documentary Fact row states it), Management Language (carried by a CP-1A row, qualified, never adopted), Analyst Interpretation (my reading of the cited basis), Insufficient Information (the basis is missing).
## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| CoreWeave is a high-risk credit: contracted revenue is long and large, but principal debt of USD 35,551 million is 8.08x LTM adjusted EBITDA, free cash flow is deeply negative and funding depends on continued market access. | Medium | Covenant levels, guarantors, financing documents and third quarter 2026 data are not in the sources, so debt capacity and recovery mechanics cannot be tested. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Remaining performance obligations of USD 103.7 billion and committed contracts at 98% of Q2 2026 revenue give long revenue visibility. | Contracted cash flows support debt service where capacity is delivered, but conversion depends on delivery. | Medium |

| Principal debt rose from USD 21,615 million to USD 35,551 million in six months, while LTM adjusted EBITDA is USD 4,400 million. | Gross leverage is 8.08x and cash interest cover is 3.35x, leaving little room for earnings shortfalls. | Medium |

| Six months 2026 free cash flow was USD (10,454) million, funded by new debt, equity placements and customer prepayments. | Debt service and growth capital depend on continued access to debt and equity markets. | High |

| Reported availability of USD 10,014 million is conditional, and USD 4,413 million of debt matures in the remainder of 2026. | Usable liquidity is lower than the USD 15,553 million headline, so refinancing risk is near term. | Medium |

| Three customers supplied 72% of Q2 2026 revenue and founder-held Class B shares carry about 66.9% of votes. | A single customer's problem would hit cash flow quickly, and creditor protection rests on unseen documents. | Medium |
### Credit view

CoreWeave, Inc. is a high-risk credit: its contracted demand is strong, but its balance sheet depends on continued access to new debt and equity. The strongest support is revenue visibility, with committed contracts at 98% of Q2 2026 revenue and remaining performance obligations of USD 103.7 billion. The weakest point is financial: principal debt of USD 35,551 million at June 30, 2026 is 8.08x LTM adjusted EBITDA, and six months 2026 free cash flow was USD (10,454) million. The outcome will be decided by delivery and funding: whether CoreWeave brings contracted capacity online on time, collects from a concentrated customer base, and refinances USD 4,413 million due in the remainder of 2026 and USD 6,184 million in 2027 while delayed-draw commitments stay conditional.
### Key findings

First, leverage is high and rising faster than earnings. CoreWeave had principal debt of USD 35,551 million at June 30, 2026 against USD 21,615 million at December 31, 2025, and LTM adjusted EBITDA of USD 4,400 million, giving 8.08x gross and 6.82x net of unrestricted cash and marketable securities, against 6.99x and 5.97x at year end [Documentary Fact; financial base]. Cash interest cover on adjusted EBITDA is 3.35x, or 2.35x against net interest expense of USD 1,874 million. Both ratios flatter the position: adjusted EBITDA adds back stock compensation, cash interest is net of capitalized interest of USD 322 million over the twelve months, and on operating income plus depreciation and amortization gross leverage is 9.46x [Analyst Interpretation]. Mechanism: debt funds assets that are not yet earning, so period-end debt over trailing earnings overstates run-rate leverage, but operating income is already negative after interest-bearing growth, with an LTM operating loss of USD (231) million and the LTM net loss is USD (1,928) million.

Second, cash flow does not cover investment. Six months 2026 operating cash flow was USD 3,663 million against purchases of property and equipment of USD 14,117 million, leaving free cash flow of USD (10,454) million; the twelve-month figure is USD (13,655) million [Documentary Fact]. The gap is funded by new debt, equity placements of USD 2.0 billion (NVIDIA, January 2026) and USD 1.0 billion (April 2026), and customer prepayments, with deferred revenue at USD 9,692 million [Documentary Fact]. Implication: the credit relies on markets staying open; a funding pause would force a cut in capital spending and slow the delivery that converts backlog to revenue.

Third, liquidity is large on paper and conditional in practice. Company-reported total liquidity was USD 15,553 million at June 30, 2026: cash USD 5,524 million, marketable securities USD 15 million and availability USD 10,014 million, which rebuilds as USD 1,967 million on the revolver, USD 385 million on DDTL 3.0, USD 5,663 million on DDTL 4.0 and USD 1,999 million on DDTL 5.0 [Documentary Fact]. Draws on the delayed-draw facilities are limited to eligible asset purchases, the DDTL 3.0 and DDTL 5.0 draw periods ended before the as-of date, and restricted cash of USD 1,380 million sits outside the figure. In August 2026, after the quarter, CoreWeave drew USD 1.2 billion on the revolver and USD 1.2 billion on the new DDTL 5.5 facility, which lowers revolver availability (USD 767 million on the financial base's indicative basis) and means cash and availability at the as-of date are Not calculable [Analyst Interpretation].

Fourth, the maturity profile is front-loaded relative to cash. Scheduled principal is USD 4,413 million in the remainder of 2026, USD 6,184 million in 2027, USD 4,416 million in 2028, USD 2,421 million in 2029, USD 3,221 million in 2030 and USD 14,896 million after that; current debt is USD 7,513 million against cash of USD 5,524 million [Documentary Fact]. Much of the near-term amount is scheduled amortization on asset-level facilities and equipment financing, which is likely to be serviced from contracted cash flows rather than refinanced [Analyst Interpretation], but DDTL 4.0 payment timing is a management estimate. Implication: near-term refinancing risk is real but concentrated in amortizing secured debt; the unsecured and convertible notes mature from 2030 onward.

Fifth, revenue visibility is strong but concentrated and delivery-dependent. Committed contracts have a weighted-average duration of about five years, remaining performance obligations are USD 103.7 billion with 41% due within 24 months, and management cites a wider backlog of about USD 104 billion plus more than USD 25 billion of commitments added in early Q3 [Documentary Fact and Management Language, kept apart]. Three customers supplied 36%, 26% and 10% of Q2 2026 revenue (72% together), customers A and B were 32% each of receivables, and customer labels change between periods, so the fall from 71% for one customer a year earlier is not a like-for-like trend [Documentary Fact]. Mechanism: take-or-pay terms fix revenue, but revenue is recognized only as capacity is delivered (393 MW undelivered at one leased site), and service credits reduce the backlog. Implication: counterparty quality of a few customers drives default risk for the asset-level facilities.

Sixth, claims outside the debt figure are large. Operating lease liabilities are USD 16,319 million, finance leases USD 221 million, leases signed but not commenced USD 35.5 billion undiscounted, joint venture funding commitments up to USD 1.7 billion, and accrued purchases USD 5,520 million [Documentary Fact]. Debt plus lease liabilities would be USD 52,091 million; no lease-adjusted ratio is offered because adjusted EBITDA is stated after operating lease cost. Implication: fixed charges will rise as leases commence, ahead of the revenue they support.

Seventh, structure and control limit what a creditor can verify. About 89.5% of principal debt is recourse (USD 31,832 million) and USD 3,719 million is non-recourse; delayed-draw facilities are secured on subsidiary assets and guaranteed by the parent except DDTL 4.0, while the notes are unsecured and guaranteed by unnamed subsidiaries [Documentary Fact]. Founders hold all Class B shares, which carry about 66.9% of votes on the cover-page counts, and no sponsor is named [Analyst Interpretation]. Mechanism: asset-level lenders hold first-priority liens on the financed equipment and cash flows, so value available to unsecured holders depends on residual value after those claims; this is a mechanic, not a recovery conclusion. Material weaknesses in internal control continued at June 30, 2026 and securities suits are pending with no accrual.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. CoreWeave has long contracted revenue: committed contracts are 98% of Q2 2026 revenue and remaining performance obligations are USD 103.7 billion with a weighted-average contract duration of about five years [Documentary Fact]. It has grown fast, with Q2 2026 revenue of USD 2,575 million against USD 1,212 million a year earlier, up 112.5%, and LTM revenue of USD 7,590 million [Documentary Fact]. It has shown access to several funding sources in 2026, including secured delayed-draw loans, unsecured notes, convertibles, a euro bond and two equity placements, which supports refinancing capacity while markets stay open [Analyst Interpretation]. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 58.0% over the last twelve months [Documentary Fact; management measure]. The asset-level structure ties each facility to financed assets and contracted cash flows, with the parent guaranteeing all but DDTL 4.0 [Documentary Fact]. Counterparties named in the sources include Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and Jane Street, with commitments of up to about USD 6.5 billion, USD 21.0 billion and USD 6.0 billion for the last three [Documentary Fact].

Weaknesses. Leverage is high: 8.08x gross and 6.82x net on adjusted EBITDA, and 9.46x gross on operating income plus depreciation and amortization [Documentary Fact]. Free cash flow is deeply negative at USD (10,454) million for six months 2026, so the business consumes external capital [Documentary Fact]. Earnings after interest are negative: the LTM operating loss is USD (231) million and net interest expense USD 1,874 million [Documentary Fact]. Refinancing and amortization are near term, with USD 4,413 million and USD 6,184 million due in the remainder of 2026 and 2027 [Documentary Fact]. Customer concentration is high, with three customers at 72% of Q2 2026 revenue [Documentary Fact]. Off-balance-sheet lease commitments of USD 35.5 billion and joint venture commitments of up to USD 1.7 billion add to future fixed charges [Documentary Fact]. Control is with founders through a ten-vote share class and no sponsor support is documented [Analyst Interpretation]. Material weaknesses in internal control continue, which weakens the reliability of figures used in lender tests [Documentary Fact]. Stockholders' equity of USD 5,024 million is small against principal debt of USD 35,551 million [Documentary Fact]. Covenant levels, guarantors and financing documents are not supplied, so headroom and legal protections cannot be tested [Insufficient Information].
### Credit assessment
| Assessment | Category | Confidence | Basis |

| Fundamental credit view: high risk. Business risk is moderate to strong on contracted revenue visibility but weakened by customer concentration and delivery dependence. Financial risk is high on leverage, negative free cash flow and funding reliance. Liquidity is adequate on a headline basis but conditional. | Analyst Interpretation | Medium (below High because covenants, guarantors and Q3 2026 data are not supplied, and the business module judged this module ready with limitations) | Financial base: leverage, cover, liquidity and maturity tables. Business and transaction context: revenue model, customer, structure, ownership and conflict registers. |

Credit thesis: CoreWeave's long, contracted, take-or-pay revenue supports a fast-growing asset-level financing model, but the heavy debt load, negative free cash flow and customer concentration make the credit dependent on on-time delivery and continued access to capital.
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity | Category |

| Funding dependence | Free cash flow of USD (10,454) million for six months 2026 is financed by new debt and equity; delayed-draw availability is conditional on asset purchases and two commitment periods ended before the as-of date | A funding pause cuts capital spending and delays the delivery that converts backlog to revenue; liquidity is lower than the headline USD 15,553 million | Critical | Documentary Fact |

| Leverage and interest burden | Principal debt USD 35,551 million is 8.08x LTM adjusted EBITDA; cash interest cover 3.35x, 2.35x on net interest expense; LTM operating loss USD (231) million | Little tolerance for an earnings shortfall or a rate rise on the floating-rate facilities | Critical | Documentary Fact |

| Near-term maturities and amortization | USD 4,413 million due in the remainder of 2026 and USD 6,184 million in 2027 against cash of USD 5,524 million | Refinancing and amortization must be met from contracted cash flows and new facilities | Material | Documentary Fact |

| Customer concentration and counterparty risk | Three customers supplied 72% of Q2 2026 revenue; customers A and B were 32% each of receivables | A delay, dispute or credit event at one customer stalls cash conversion for the asset-level facilities | Material | Documentary Fact |

| Delivery and execution | Backlog converts only as capacity is delivered; 393 MW remain undelivered at one leased site and 355 MW at other lease sites; supplier dependence on NVIDIA GPUs | Delivery delays defer revenue while rent, depreciation and interest accrue | Material | Documentary Fact |

| Lease and commitment burden | Operating lease liabilities USD 16,319 million; leases not commenced USD 35.5 billion; joint venture commitments up to USD 1.7 billion | Fixed charges rise ahead of related revenue and sit outside reported debt | Material | Documentary Fact |

| Structure, guarantees and control | Asset-level liens on financed equipment; notes unsecured with unnamed guarantors; founder voting control; no sponsor | Protection depends on documents not supplied; this is a mechanic, not a recovery conclusion | Material | Analyst Interpretation |

| Reporting and litigation | Material weaknesses in internal control continued at June 30, 2026; securities and derivative suits pending, no accrual and no estimate | Reliability of figures used in lender tests and a possible unquantified claim | Minor | Documentary Fact |
## Calculations

No new calculation was made. Every figure comes from the financial base or the business and transaction context handoffs. Where this module combines handoff figures it uses their stated results: the 72% customer share (36%, 26% and 10%), the 89.5% recourse share, the 66.9% voting share, the USD 767 million indicative revolver availability and the USD 52,091 million debt plus lease liabilities.
## Gaps
| Gap | Why it matters | What it affects | Severity | Action |

| Covenant levels, definitions and headroom: Not supplied | Maintenance tests and sizing limits decide when lenders can accelerate or stop funding | Liquidity, leverage tolerance, default risk | Critical | Obtain the credit agreements and compliance certificates; headroom is Not calculable |

| Financing documents (indentures, credit agreements, guarantees) and guarantor list: Not supplied | They set liens, guarantees, restricted payments and ranking | Loss given default mechanics, structure | Critical | Obtain the exhibits listed in the filings |

| Third quarter 2026 results and cash, debt and liquidity at the as-of date: Not calculable | August 2026 draws changed availability; DDTL 3.0 and DDTL 5.0 draw periods ended | Liquidity, refinancing | Critical | Obtain the third quarter 2026 report and any later filings |

| Customer contract terms (termination rights, pricing, remedies) and current top-customer identity: Not supplied | They determine backlog quality and concentration | Revenue durability | Material | Obtain contract summaries or management disclosure |

| Ownership percentages, ratings and guidance: Not supplied | They affect control, pricing and forward cash flow | Control, market access | Material | Obtain the proxy statement, ratings and the earnings call |

| Logged conflicts not reconciled: backlog versus remaining performance obligations; DDTL 5.0 and DDTL 2.1 maturity dates; customer labels across periods | They change how much backlog is firm and when some maturities fall | Revenue visibility, maturity wall | Minor | Treat the filed remaining performance obligations as controlling; confirm dates in the agreements |

| Monitoring inputs: debt-by-entity schedule, sizing calculations, add-back bridge: Not supplied | Needed to monitor headroom between filings | Monitoring posture | Material | Request them from the company |

Inherited from the upstream modules: source readiness was ready with limitations, the financial base is restricted by the missing covenant data, and the business module judged this module ready with limitations, which is why confidence is below High.
## Next module
Proceed to the evidence trace review (CP-5) over all four modules. It should check that:
1. Each CP-1 figure used here (principal debt, adjusted EBITDA, leverage, cover, free cash flow, liquidity, maturities, leases) resolves to the same value, period and unit in the financial base.

2. Each business fact used here (revenue model, customer shares, structure, voting, conflicts) resolves to a tagged row in the business and transaction context, and that management claims stay tagged as Management Language.
3. The four logged conflicts and the Not supplied items stay open and are not treated as resolved.
4. No text states a peer ranking, an instrument recommendation or an expected recovery outcome.
